description: Original reading passages for read_passage (WORKBOOK_SPEC 8.5), two or so per grade, fiction and nonfiction, each with its questions.

red_hen_hat.description: A three-sentence story for a grown-up to read aloud; the child circles answers.
red_hen_hat.title: The Red Hat
red_hen_hat.text: Pip has a red hat. The wind takes the hat. Pip runs and gets it back.

big_dog.description: A very short decodable story about a dog who digs, with two picture-free questions.
big_dog.title: The Big Dog
big_dog.text: I see a big dog. The dog can dig. The dog digs a hole. Look! The dog has a bone.

rain_day.description: A short story about playing inside on a rainy day.
rain_day.title: Rain, Rain
rain_day.text: It is a wet day. Mom and I stay in. We make a fort with a big sheet. We read in the fort. It is fun!

frog_jump.description: A short story about a frog who learns to jump to a lily pad; questions on detail and feeling.
frog_jump.title: Little Frog
frog_jump.text: Little Frog sat by the pond. He wanted to jump to the lily pad, but it looked far. His sister said, "Bend your legs and push!" Little Frog tried. Splash! He fell in. He tried again and again. At last he landed on the lily pad. He felt proud.

questions.q: How did he feel at the end?
What did he do after he fell in?

bees_busy.description: A short nonfiction text about honeybees; questions on facts.
bees_busy.title: Busy Bees
bees_busy.text: Bees live in a hive. Many bees live together. Bees fly from flower to flower. They drink nectar. Bees use nectar to make honey. Bees also carry pollen. This helps new plants grow.

lost_mitten.description: A story about a girl who finds her lost mitten by retracing her steps; sequence and inference.
lost_mitten.title: The Lost Mitten
lost_mitten.text: After recess, Rosa had only one blue mitten. She looked in her coat pocket. It was empty. Then she thought about her morning. First she had played on the slide. Next she built a snowman with Jay. Rosa ran to the snowman. There was her mitten, stuck on its nose! Jay laughed. "Our snowman wanted to stay warm," he said.

questions.q: What did she do first at recess?
Why did Rosa think about her morning?
questions.answer: To remember where she had been.

seeds_travel.description: A nonfiction text about how seeds travel by wind, water and animals.
seeds_travel.title: How Seeds Travel
seeds_travel.text: Plants cannot walk, but their seeds can travel far. Some seeds are light and fluffy. The wind carries them away. Some seeds float on water to a new shore. Other seeds have tiny hooks. They stick to animal fur and ride along. When a seed lands in good soil, it can grow into a new plant.

science_fair.description: A story about a boy whose science fair plan fails and who learns from it; character and theme.
science_fair.title: The Volcano That Wouldn't
science_fair.text: Omar had practised his model volcano all week. On the day of the science fair, he poured in the vinegar and waited. Nothing happened. Kids began to walk away. Omar's face felt hot. Then he noticed the baking soda box was still full; he had forgotten the main ingredient. Instead of hiding, he explained to the judges what went wrong and why the mix needs both parts. One judge smiled. "A good scientist learns from mistakes," she said. Omar got a ribbon for the best explanation.

questions.q: Why didn't the volcano work at first?
How did Omar feel when kids walked away?
What is a lesson of the story?
What did Omar do instead of hiding?

octopus.description: A nonfiction text about octopuses' clever ways to hide and escape.
octopus.title: Masters of Disguise
octopus.text: The octopus is one of the cleverest animals in the sea. It has no bones, so it can squeeze through a gap the size of a coin. Special cells in its skin let it change colour in less than a second. It can look like sand, rock or coral. If a hunter gets too close, an octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink and jet away. Scientists have even seen octopuses open jars to reach food inside.

questions.q: Why can an octopus squeeze through tiny gaps?
What does the ink help it do?
What does disguise mean in the title?
Name two ways an octopus stays safe.
questions.answer: It changes colour and squirts ink.

town_garden.description: A story about neighbours turning an empty lot into a garden; problem, solution and point of view.
town_garden.title: The Empty Lot
town_garden.text: For years, the lot on Maple Street was full of weeds and broken bottles. Nadia passed it every day on her way to school and wondered what it could become. One spring she wrote a letter to the city council asking if the neighbourhood could plant a garden there. The council agreed, but only if people promised to care for it. Nadia knocked on doors. Mr. Lee offered tools, the Garcia family brought seedlings, and the school donated old rain barrels. By summer, rows of tomatoes and sunflowers filled the lot, and neighbours who had never spoken were trading recipes over the fence.

questions.q: What problem did Nadia want to solve?
What did the council ask for?
options: a promise to care for it

questions.q: How did the garden change the neighbourhood?
questions.answer: Neighbours got to know each other.

monarch.description: A nonfiction text about the monarch butterfly's long migration; cause, effect and text evidence.
monarch.title: The Long Flight
monarch.text: Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies leave Canada and the northern United States. They fly as far as 4,000 kilometres to the mountain forests of central Mexico. No single butterfly makes the round trip. The monarchs that fly south live up to eight months, much longer than summer monarchs, which live only a few weeks. In spring they head north, lay eggs on milkweed plants and die. Their great-grandchildren will make the journey south again, finding the same forests they have never seen. Scientists think monarchs use the position of the Sun and the Earth's magnetism to find their way.

questions.q: Which plant do monarchs lay eggs on?
How are the autumn monarchs different?
How might monarchs find their way?
questions.answer: By using the Sun and Earth's magnetism.

inventor_letter.description: A story told in a letter from a young inventor; point of view, theme and word meaning.
inventor_letter.title: Dear Grandpa
inventor_letter.text: Dear Grandpa, You always said that every invention starts with an annoyance. Mine started with my little brother's shoelaces, which came undone eleven times on our walk to school. I designed a clip that holds the bow in place. My first model, carved from an eraser, snapped. The second, made from a bottle cap, was too bulky. The third, printed at the library, finally worked, but only on flat laces. I was discouraged until I remembered your workshop and the shelf of failed gadgets you called your teachers. So I am on version four. Ask me next month how many times Leo's laces came undone. Love, Priya

questions.q: Why did Grandpa call failed gadgets his teachers?
What is the theme of the letter?
questions.answer: Keep trying and learn from failures.

coral_reef.description: A nonfiction text on coral reefs, why they matter and what threatens them; main idea and evidence.
coral_reef.title: Cities Under the Sea
coral_reef.text: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet about a quarter of all ocean species depend on them. A reef looks like rock, but it is built by tiny animals called coral polyps. Each polyp makes a hard skeleton, and over thousands of years the skeletons pile into huge structures. Many corals get their colour and much of their food from algae that live inside them. When ocean water gets too warm, the coral pushes the algae out and turns white, which is called bleaching. Bleached coral can recover if the water cools, but long heat waves can kill whole reefs. Scientists are now growing young coral in nurseries and planting it back on damaged reefs.

questions.q: What are scientists doing to help reefs?
questions.answer: Growing young coral and planting it on reefs.
